chapters.title: Chapter 1 — What this game is
chapters.body:
You are an Investigating Officer of the Metro Crime Branch. This is not a puzzle with a correct answer hidden in a dialogue tree. It is an investigation, and it will be decided by what you can lawfully prove.

The single most important idea:
  A fact you discover is worth NOTHING until it is written into a record, seized under a lawful memo, kept in an unbroken chain of custody, and admissible under the law of evidence.

A brilliant deduction that lives only in your head cannot convict anyone. Everything in this game flows from that sentence.

You will begin by applying for the post. You will be interviewed. You will be inducted, given an assistant, and handed your first case. You will register an FIR, process a crime scene, send exhibits for forensic examination, interrogate suspects, recover what they disclose, assemble a charge sheet, and see your work tested in court. Then you will be judged, and your department will know exactly what kind of officer you are.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 — The clock (and why you cannot do everything)
chapters.body:
Your case has a deadline fixed by law. For offences punishable up to ten years it is 60 days; for graver offences, 90. On the day it expires, the accused becomes entitled to bail on default and your case dies. This is BNSS s.187, and it is not negotiable.

Every action costs days:
  · Processing the scene — 1 to 2 days
  · Each forensic test — 3 to 21 days depending on the test
  · A CDR, ANPR or CCTV pull — 2 to 4 days
  · Financial analysis — 5 to 8 days
  · Each interrogation session — 1 day
  · Charge sheet drafting — 2 to 3 days

You cannot test every exhibit or chase every lead. The real puzzle of this game is deciding what you can afford to prove. Spend your days on the evidence that goes to the heart of the offence, and let the rest go.

The HUD at the top of the screen always shows your day and your deadline. When it turns amber you have fifteen days left. When it turns red you have seven.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 — The FIR (Act 1)
chapters.body:
Every case begins in the Duty Room. A complaint arrives. You write the FIR yourself, in your own words.

Under BNSS s.173 you must register an FIR for every cognizable offence. The classification system will check your narrative against the statutory ingredients of the offence and tell you which ingredients you have established and which you have not. Emotional writing scores nothing here; ingredients score.

Write what you were told. Give the date, the time and the exact place. If there was a delay before reporting, explain it — an unexplained delay is the first thing the defence will find.

You have one significant choice. For offences punishable between three and seven years you may, with the permission of the Superintendent of Police, conduct a preliminary inquiry of up to fourteen days to see whether there is really a case (BNSS s.173(3)). It buys certainty and costs you a fortnight of your clock. It is not available for the gravest offences. Choosing wrongly is a scored decision, so read the section in the Legal Library before you decide.

If you refuse to register a genuine cognizable offence, the complainant is entitled to take it over your head to the Superintendent, and you will lose standing in the department.

chapters.title: Chapter 4 — The crime scene (Act 2)
chapters.body:
Attend the scene and process it in the right order. The order matters more than you might think.

  1. Log your arrival — time, weather, who was already there.
  2. Establish the cordon, then walk the scene before touching anything.
  3. Photograph it: wide, mid, macro, with a scale reference.
  4. Draw your scene diagram and give every find a grid reference.
  5. Examine and record the exhibits.
  6. Canvass the neighbourhood for witnesses.
  7. SEAL the scene.

Some items are invisible in ordinary light. A UV lamp or an alternate light source will reveal what your eye missed — but those tools cost time, and time is your clock.

Then the most important step in the whole act, and the one most often botched:

  THE SEIZURE MEMO. Under BNSS s.103, every seizure must be made in the presence of TWO OR MORE INDEPENDENT AND RESPECTABLE INHABITANTS OF THE LOCALITY, and a signed list prepared.

The game will check your witnesses. If you record only one, or the same person twice, or a police officer, the exhibit is TAINTED. Permanently. It will never be admissible, no exhibit is repairable after the fact, and the Court will be told. This is not a small penalty; a tainted exhibit is worse than no exhibit, because it invites the defence to attack your whole file.

Every exhibit you seize begins a chain of custody. Each hand-off is logged. A gap in that chain makes the exhibit contestable, even if the seizure itself was perfect.

chapters.title: Chapter 5 — Forensics (Act 3)
chapters.body:
Untested evidence is weak evidence. But the laboratory is not free: every test consumes days from your clock, and some tests are slow. DNA profiling takes about eighteen days. Fingerprint examination about four. You must choose.

Each report is written with a confidence figure and, where the exhibit was handled badly, a stated limitation. Read the limitations. They are the exact words the defence will quote.

Two rules govern this act.

First, the chain of custody. When an exhibit goes to the laboratory and returns, that movement must be logged. If it is not, the exhibit becomes contestable no matter how conclusive the science is.

Second, and this is the rule that ends more digital cases than any other — the BSA s.63 certificate. Any electronic record, whether CCTV, call detail records, a device image or a bank data extract, is admissible ONLY IF accompanied by a certificate:
  · identifying the record, including its hash,
  · describing how it was produced,
  · giving the particulars of the device,
  · and dealing with the conditions that ensure accuracy and integrity,
  signed by BOTH the person in charge of the record AND an expert.

One signature is not enough. If you send digital evidence to court without that dual-signed certificate, the court will not even look at it. Hash the record, then have the certificate completed and signed by two different people.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 — Working the case (Act 4)
chapters.body:
Now you investigate. The tool you have is time, and you do not have much of it.

  · Statements — record what people actually told you, under BNSS s.180. Do not put your own conclusions into someone else's mouth. When that witness later departs from the statement, the defence will show that the words were yours and the statement becomes worthless.
  · Surveillance pulls — CCTV, call detail records, ANPR, financial records. Each returns leads if the source has anything, and nothing if it does not.
  · Alibi verification — when a name sits in your file, verify the alibi. A false lead who owns the matching vehicle and appears in the money trail will ruin your case if you charge him without checking. A verified alibi is also valuable: it eliminates a suspect and makes you look competent.
  · Informatics — cheap, fast, and occasionally invented. Treat informer information as a lead to be verified, never as proof.
  · The Test Identification Parade — where identity is genuinely in issue. Conduct it promptly, place the accused among persons of similar description, and have it supervised independently. Never let the witness see the accused beforehand. A mistaken identification is worse than no identification.

The Case Diary is your record of all this. Write in it. It is the document the court reads to see what you did and when.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 — Interrogation (Act 5) — the most important lesson
chapters.body:
This is the heart of the game, and the place where most players first fail. Read this chapter twice.

Type whatever questions you like. The suspect is a person with his own interests, fears and lies. If you bully him he closes up. If you build rapport, or present something that genuinely traps him, he may concede part of the truth.

But here is the rule that decides cases. Under BSA s.23:

  A CONFESSION TO A POLICE OFFICER IS NOT PROVABLE.

So much of the information received from a person in custody as relates DISTINCTLY TO THE FACT THEREBY DISCOVERED may be proved — but only if the discovery was made in the presence of a Magistrate or in the presence of two or more respectable witnesses.

In plain terms: it does not matter what he tells you. What matters is whether what he told you led you to find something real, in the right way, before the right witnesses.

This means:
  · "He told me he did it." — Worth nothing. Ever.
  · "He told me where the weapon was. I took him there. We recovered it. Two respectable persons watched and signed." — That part is provable.

So the best interrogation is not one that extracts a confession. It is one that extracts a LOCATION or a THING. A place to dig, a tank to look behind, a cot to look under.

When you close an interrogation, the game will apply s.23 to everything that was said and show you two columns: what is provable, and what is not. That split is your real result. Then you must go and execute the recovery — see the next chapter.

Tactics lose their power when repeated. A bluff is high-risk: it may work once, and if it is exposed your credibility collapses.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 — Recovery (Act 6) — where talk becomes evidence
chapters.body:
A disclosure is not evidence. A recovery is.

When a suspect discloses a locatable fact, a lead appears on your Evidence Board. You must execute the recovery: go to the place, find the thing, and do it in the presence of two respectable witnesses.

If you do, the information becomes provable under BSA s.23 to the extent of the fact discovered. If you do not — or if you recover the object without witnesses — the information remains a confession to a police officer and proves nothing at all.

This is the single highest-value step in the game. A case built on a properly witnessed recovery plus admissible physical evidence is a conviction. A case built on what a man said in a room is an acquittal with a pointed judgment about your competence.

Do not neglect to link the recovery to the accused in your records. A recovered object proves a fact; your file must show whose information produced it.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 — The charge sheet (Act 7)
chapters.body:
Under BNSS s.193 you send the court a report setting out the parties, the offences, the witnesses, the exhibits and documents, and the brief facts of the case. The court then decides whether to take cognizance.

Compose it carefully. The court's scrutiny desk will check:
  · whether the offences you have charged are made out on the ADMISSIBLE evidence;
  · whether every listed exhibit is admissible;
  · whether every listed witness has a recorded statement;
  · whether each accused has a proper role attributed to him;
  · whether the narrative is coherent and charges nothing that no exhibit supports.

Five defects lose cases. Learn them now:
  1. OVER-CHARGING — charging murder where your proof supports culpable homicide. It weakens your case and the court will say so.
  2. LISTING A TAINTED OR INADMISSIBLE EXHIBIT — the defence's easiest opening. If you know an exhibit is defective, say so in your file rather than pretended otherwise; but do not list it as proof.
  3. LISTING A WITNESS WHOSE STATEMENT YOU NEVER RECORDED.
  4. AN ACCUSED LIST WITHOUT ROLE ATTRIBUTION.
  5. A NARRATIVE THAT CHARGES SOMETHING NO EXHIBIT SUPPORTS.

If the court returns your report unreceived, you may cure the defect and resubmit — if there is time left on the clock. Often there is not.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 — Trial (Act 8)
chapters.body:
Your file is now tested. Defence counsel will go through it looking for the gaps you left, and they will find them in this order:

  · Every tainted seizure,
  · Every uncertified electronic record,
  · Every break in the chain of custody,
  · Every witness whose statement does not match his evidence,
  · Every doubt that survives against the prosecution.

The court will expressly disregard tainted and inadmissible material, and will say in the judgment which exhibits it rejected and why. Then it will decide on what remains.

You will write your own summary of arguments before the verdict, and the court will consider it. Write it as an argument, not a story: deal with your own weaknesses first, because the court has already found them.

The possible verdicts are Conviction, Partial (a lesser offence made out on the same facts), and Acquittal. An acquittal is not a failure of the game; it is the honest result of a case that was not proved. You will receive a written judgment naming exactly what was wrong. Read it. It is the most useful document in the game.

The judgment's remarks are tied to your file. Fix the defects it names in your next case and your standing rises.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 — Your team and the messaging desk
chapters.body:
At induction you are assigned an assistant, Junior Constable Ravi Deshmukh, who stays with you for your whole career. He runs errands, collects reports, serves summonses and verifies alibis — and he will tell you when he has made a mistake.

As your standing rises you may appoint more officers from the candidate pool. Composition genuinely changes the game:
  · A Forensic Analyst improves laboratory turnaround and can spot contamination.
  · A Cyber Cell Operative produces clean hash-and-certificate chains and can sign the s.63 certificate.
  · A Field Constable canvasses faster and serves summonses.
  · A Legal Advisor tells you how the defence will open your file, and warns you before you over-charge.
  · An Informant Handler improves informer quality.
  · A Document or Ballistics Expert can dismantle an overreaching laboratory report.

The messaging desk holds a thread for every person, plus a thread for the Head of Branch, your senior, the laboratory desk, the court reader, and one squad thread per case.

Messages are not decoration. What you ask for creates real state:
  · Ask the Head for additional time and he may grant days — or refuse, and tell you why.
  · Ask for a warrant and he will weigh whether your file justifies it.
  · Ask your assistant to canvass an area and he will be occupied for the days it takes.

Your Assistant, your senior and the Head are career-wide threads: they are the same people across every case you hold, so a message about one case and a message about another live in the same conversation. Squad threads are per-case and follow whichever case you have open.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 — Running more than one case
chapters.body:
Once your rank allows it you may hold several cases at once. The Case Wall shows them all as physical files, each with its own colour tab, its own day counter and its own deadline.

Switch a case and every desk on screen re-reads itself from that case. There is no risk of confusing them: nothing on screen is shared except your career and your people.

But your PEOPLE are shared, and that is the strategic tension. The clock is per case, yet your assistant, your specialists, the laboratory capacity and your budget are singular. If you send Ravi to canvass in one case, he is unavailable for your other case until he finishes.

So a player holding three cases is really playing one game of resource allocation across three deadlines. Assign your best specialist to the case that will die first. Do the slow laboratory work early. And use the squad threads to keep each case's work separate — while remembering that your senior and your Head see everything.

Cross-case intelligence is possible and rewarded: if the same name surfaces in two files, link them on your Evidence Board and tell your senior. Career statistics aggregate across everything you close.

chapters.title: Chapter 13 — Settings, assistance, and how it affects your record
chapters.body:
Settings is where you decide how much help you want, and it is not a switch you can hide behind. Every assistance option that steers you reduces the standing you earn when the case closes. That is deliberate: an officer who solves a case unaided is worth more to the Branch than one who needed the answers.

ASSISTANCE
  · Legal Guidance — puts the relevant sections and explanations beside every form. Costs 5%.
  · Procedure Coach — step checklists and blocking-item prompts per act. Costs 5%.
  · Interrogation Aid — tactical hints during questioning. Costs 10%.
  · Evidence Analysis Aid — "what to look for" hints at the scene and in the laboratory. Costs 10%.
  · Charge-Framing Aid — suggests sections and warns about over-charging. Costs 8%.
  · Consequence Preview — tells you what will happen before you commit. Costs 5%.
  · Auto-Highlight Statutory Ingredients — live chips as you write the FIR. No cost.
  · Notepad Suggestions — the notepad files observations for you. No cost.

ON-DEMAND HELP
  · The "Guide me" button on any screen explains the procedure for that exact screen. This one is free, because asking how a form works is not the same as being told the answer.

DIFFICULTY is set per case when you open it and cannot be changed afterwards.

THE LEGAL LIBRARY contains every section the game uses, with the bare law, a plain-English explanation, and a note on how it is used here. The FORMS CODEX describes every document, field by field, with the pitfalls that lose cases.

THE PLAYER GUIDE is the document you are reading.

chapters.title: Chapter 14 — The investigating officer's checklist
chapters.body:
Keep this beside you. Twenty-two questions, in order, that a competent officer answers before filing.

BEFORE THE FIR
  1. Is the offence cognizable? If yes, an FIR must be registered. There is no discretion.
  2. Does my narrative establish the statutory ingredients of the offence?
  3. Have I recorded the date, time and place precisely? Do they match everything I will record later?
  4. If there was delay in reporting, have I recorded the explanation?

AT THE SCENE
  5. Did I cordon, walk through, photograph and diagram before I touched anything?
  6. Does every exhibit have a grid reference?
  7. Did I use UV or an alternate light source where the scene might hide a trace?
  8. Did I canvass for witnesses?
  9. HAVE I SEIZED EACH EXHIBIT BEFORE TWO INDEPENDENT WITNESSES? (If not, the exhibit is lost.)
 10. Is each item described so precisely that it will still be identifiable in court, years from now?

FORENSICS
 11. Have I chosen the tests that go to the heart of the offence, given my remaining days?
 12. Is the chain of custody logged for every movement to and from the laboratory?
 13. For every electronic record: is it hashed, and is there a DUAL-SIGNED s.63 certificate?

INVESTIGATION
 14. Has every person in my file given a statement, recorded in their own words rather than mine?
 15. Have I verified the alibi of anyone I might charge?
 16. Where identity is in issue, was the identification parade fair and independently supervised?

INTERROGATION AND RECOVERY
 17. Did I extract a LOCATION or a THING, or only talk?
 18. Have I converted every disclosure into a witnessed physical recovery?
 19. Have I recorded the recovery against the person whose information produced it?

FILING
 20. Have I charged only what the admissible evidence supports?
 21. Is every exhibit I have listed admissible?
 22. Does my narrative tie every charged offence to at least one admissible item of proof?

If any answer is no, do not file yet — unless the clock has left you no choice, in which case file and be honest about the weakness in the file itself.

forms.title: First Information Report
forms.when_used: Immediately on receiving information of a cognizable offence.
forms.fields_json:
[{"field":"Police Station / District","guidance":"Pre-filled. Verify jurisdiction — if the scene is outside your station limits, you must transfer, not invent jurisdiction.","required":1},
   {"field":"FIR Number","guidance":"Assigned by the system on successful registration. Format DD/YY/NNN.","required":0},
   {"field":"Act & Section(s)","guidance":"The offence you believe is made out. At registration stage this may be provisional — but it must match the ingredients in your narrative.","required":1},
   {"field":"Date & Time of Occurrence","guidance":"Must be consistent with everything you will record later. A mismatch here is a permanent contradiction the defence will find.","required":1},
   {"field":"Place of Occurrence","guidance":"Exact location. Drives which Crime Scene layout loads.","required":1},
   {"field":"Complainant / Informant details","guidance":"Name, age, address, occupation, contact. If information is oral it is reduced to writing and read back.","required":1},
   {"field":"Narrative (the substance)","guidance":"Write what you were told, in sequence, using first person where the informant spoke. Include, for each ingredient of the offence, the fact that satisfies it. Do not editorialise, do not conclude.","required":1},
   {"field":"Delay in reporting","guidance":"If there was delay, record the cause. Unexplained delay is an early defence point.","required":0},
   {"field":"Signature of Informant","guidance":"Read over and signed. Free copy handed over.","required":1}]
forms.pitfalls: The three classic defects: (1) narrative that does not satisfy a single statutory ingredient; (2) mismatch between the stated offence and the facts; (3) failure to record an explanation for delay.

forms.title: Seizure / Recovery Memo
forms.when_used: Whenever anything is taken into custody from a scene, person or premises.
forms.fields_json:
[{"field":"Memo Number & Date","guidance":"Sequential. Never back-date.","required":1},
   {"field":"Place of search / seizure","guidance":"Exact address and, for a scene, the grid reference of the found location.","required":1},
   {"field":"Time of commencement and conclusion","guidance":"Recorded to the minute, both entries.","required":1},
   {"field":"List of items seized","guidance":"Describe each item so it is identifiable years later — make, model, colour, condition, quantity, pack size.","required":1},
   {"field":"Independent Witness 1","guidance":"An adult resident of the locality, not a police officer, not a party to the case.","required":1},
   {"field":"Independent Witness 2","guidance":"A second, different, independent person. Two witnesses is a statutory minimum, not a target.","required":1},
   {"field":"Packing / sealing details","guidance":"How each item was packed, sealed and labelled. Enables the chain of custody to begin cleanly.","required":1},
   {"field":"Signature of IO and witnesses","guidance":"All three sign the same sheet at the same time.","required":1}]
forms.pitfalls: The many ways to lose an exhibit forever: only one witness; a witness who is a police officer; the same person entered twice; no grid reference; a vague description that could be anything; back-dating. Any of these taints the exhibit and it can never be repaired.

forms.title: Chain of Custody Record
forms.when_used: From the moment of seizure to production in court.
forms.fields_json:
[{"field":"Exhibit reference","guidance":"Same identifier as the seizure memo.","required":1},
   {"field":"Each hand-off: from, to, date, time, purpose","guidance":"Every single movement — to malkhana, to FSL, back, to court. A missing link breaks continuity.","required":1},
   {"field":"Seal condition on each transfer","guidance":"State whether the seal was intact at each hand-off.","required":1},
   {"field":"Signature of receiving officer","guidance":"Each hand-off countersigned.","required":1}]
forms.pitfalls: The usual failure is the unlogged transfer — the exhibit goes to the lab and comes back with no record of who carried it.

forms.title: Certificate for Electronic Records
forms.when_used: For EVERY electronic record — CCTV, CDR, IPDR, phone images, emails, bank data extracts.
forms.fields_json:
[{"field":"Description of the electronic record","guidance":"What it is, its hash, and the device or system it came from.","required":1},
   {"field":"Date and time of production","guidance":"When the copy was made.","required":1},
   {"field":"Particulars of the device","guidance":"Make, model, serial, storage medium, and that it was in lawful control.","required":1},
   {"field":"Conditions ensuring accuracy and integrity","guidance":"That the device was operating properly, that the record was produced in the ordinary course, and that no tampering occurred.","required":1},
   {"field":"Signature of person in charge","guidance":"The person occupying a responsible position in relation to the device or the record.","required":1},
   {"field":"Signature of expert","guidance":"The forensic expert. Two signatures are required — a single signature is defective.","required":1}]
forms.pitfalls: Rendering the exhibit inadmissible without any argument: not certifying it at all, certifying with one signature, certifying a record whose hash you never took.

forms.title: Inquest Report
forms.fields_json:
[{"field":"Place, date and hour of inquest","guidance":"Where the body was and when you attended.","required":1},
   {"field":"Before whom held","guidance":"The officer holding it, rank and station.","required":1},
   {"field":"Name, sex, age of the deceased","guidance":"As known; note if unidentified.","required":1},
   {"field":"Apparent cause of death","guidance":"What you SAW — injuries, position, condition. An opinion at inquest is not a post-mortem finding; do not confuse them.","required":1},
   {"field":"Witnesses examined","guidance":"Persons who identified the body or know the circumstances.","required":1},
   {"field":"Body forwarded for post-mortem","guidance":"To which hospital, by whom, seal reference.","required":1}]
forms.pitfalls: Stating the cause of death as a certainty at inquest. At this stage you record apparent cause; the post-mortem decides.

forms.title: Test Identification Parade
forms.when_used: Where identity of the accused is in issue and the witness did not previously know him.
forms.fields_json:
[{"field":"Case and date","guidance":"Parade held during investigation, promptly. Delay weakens it.","required":1},
   {"field":"Identifying witnesses","guidance":"Witnesses who claimed to have seen the accused.","required":1},
   {"field":"Dummies and sequence","guidance":"The accused placed among persons of similar description. Record how many and their descriptions.","required":1},
   {"field":"Result per witness","guidance":"Whether each witness identified the accused, and with what certainty.","required":1},
   {"field":"Conducting Magistrate / officer","guidance":"Independent supervision is essential — police conducting a parade themselves is fatal to its value.","required":1}]
forms.pitfalls: Showing the witness a photo of the accused first, or letting the witness see him before the parade. Both destroy the identification evidence.

forms.title: Remand / Production Report
forms.when_used: On arrest, and at each remand hearing.
forms.fields_json:
[{"field":"Grounds of arrest","guidance":"The necessity test, recorded in writing.","required":1},
   {"field":"Particulars communicated","guidance":"Confirm the accused was told the offence and the grounds, and his bail right.","required":1},
   {"field":"Medical examination","guidance":"Whether conducted and the time.","required":1},
   {"field":"Production before Magistrate","guidance":"Within 24 hours excluding journey time.","required":1},
   {"field":"Custody sought and reason","guidance":"Why further custody is necessary for the investigation.","required":1}]
forms.pitfalls: Missing the 24-hour production window, or arresting without recording the necessity grounds.

forms.title: Charge Sheet / Final Report
forms.when_used: On completion of investigation, within 60 or 90 days.
forms.fields_json:
[{"field":"FIR and case particulars","guidance":"Number, date, station, offences.","required":1},
   {"field":"Names of parties","guidance":"Complainant, victim, accused with full particulars and role attribution.","required":1},
   {"field":"Offences made out","guidance":"The BNS/BSA/allied sections you say are made out on the evidence — not on your belief.","required":1},
   {"field":"List of witnesses","guidance":"Each witness with what they will prove. A witness on the list whose statement you never recorded is a defect.","required":1},
   {"field":"List of exhibits / documents","guidance":"ONLY those admissible with an intact chain. Listing a tainted exhibit invites the defence's first attack.","required":1},
   {"field":"Brief facts of the case","guidance":"A coherent factual narrative that ties every charged offence to at least one admissible item of proof.","required":1},
   {"field":"Arrest and custody particulars","guidance":"Whether arrested, when, and present custody.","required":1},
   {"field":"Memo of evidence / annexures","guidance":"Statements under s.180, seizure memos, FSL reports, s.63 certificates, medical reports, TIP.","required":1}]
forms.pitfalls: The five defects that lose cases: over-charging; listing inadmissible exhibits; witnesses whose statements you never recorded; an accused list without role attribution; a narrative that charges something no exhibit supports.

forms.title: Application for Search Warrant
forms.when_used: Where the place to be searched is not covered by the FIR or is not voluntarily open to you.
forms.fields_json:
[{"field":"Premises and occupant","guidance":"Exact address and who occupies it.","required":1},
   {"field":"What is sought","guidance":"Specific things connected with the offence.","required":1},
   {"field":"Why the warrant is necessary","guidance":"What attempts have been made, and why the person will not voluntarily produce.","required":1},
   {"field":"Grounds to believe it is there","guidance":"The information that leads you to the premises — a lead, a recovery, a statement.","required":1}]
forms.pitfalls: Saying only "we suspect". A warrant must be tied to a specific, recorded lead — otherwise anything found is challengeable.

forms.title: Witness Statement (s.180 BNSS)
forms.when_used: When recording a person's account of the facts.
forms.fields_json:
[{"field":"Witness particulars","guidance":"Name, age, address, relationship to parties.","required":1},
   {"field":"Date, time, place of recording","guidance":"","required":1},
   {"field":"The statement itself","guidance":"The witness's OWN account in sequence, in his voice. Your inferences must not appear. Separately, only the core may later be signed.","required":1},
   {"field":"Signature","guidance":"Only the portion admissible is signed.","required":1}]
forms.pitfalls: Mixing your conclusions into the witness's statement. When he later departs from it, the defence will show that the words were yours all along — and the statement becomes worthless.

refs.title: Prohibition and punishment for contravention involving narcotics
refs.plain: The narcotics law, separate from the BNS. Quantity seized decides the severity band.
refs.in_game: Tier 5 branch. The quantity recovered (a lab-weighed fact) sets the punishment band, so the seizure and weighing protocol must be perfect.

refs.title: Damage to computer resource / computer related offences
refs.plain: Hacking and data offences sit under the IT Act alongside BNS cheating.
refs.in_game: Cyber branch charging: BNS s.318 plus IT Act sections for the intrusion itself.

refs.title: Requirements for accidents and vehicle identification
refs.plain: Road accident reporting and vehicle tracing duties.
refs.in_game: Roadside scene branch: chassis/engine number and ANPR tracing feed identity proof.

refs.title: Punishment for murder
refs.plain: Murder carries the heaviest penalty; the framing must be exact.
refs.in_game: Available in the Charge Sheet offence picker for the homicide branch. Over-charging it on a weaker set of facts hurts you.

refs.title: Punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder
refs.plain: A lesser homicide charge than murder — used where the intention is not fully established.
refs.in_game: The "partial conviction" path: if your proof supports the lesser charge, this is what the court convicts under instead of acquitting.

refs.title: Voluntarily causing hurt
refs.plain: The basic assault charge.
refs.in_game: Used in the assault branch and as a lesser included offence.

refs.title: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt
refs.plain: A more serious assault charge where the injury is grievous.
refs.in_game: Depends on the medical report grading the injury — a lab dependency.

refs.title: Theft
refs.plain: Taking someone's property without consent is theft.
refs.in_game: Tier 1 branch. The FIR classifier expects the ingredients of dishonest intention and movable property.

refs.title: Robbery
refs.plain: Theft with force or threat of immediate force becomes robbery — a serious charge.
refs.in_game: Tier 2 branch; escalates the day limit to 90 days and raises the standard of proof.

refs.title: Criminal breach of trust
refs.plain: Someone trusted with property took it for themselves.
refs.in_game: Financial branch; depends on document examination and account forensics.

refs.title: Cheating
refs.plain: Lying to someone to get their property or their consent.
refs.in_game: Cyber and financial branches; pairs with s.316 and digital evidence.

refs.title: Criminal conspiracy
refs.plain: An agreement to commit a crime is itself an offence.
refs.in_game: Narcotics and organised branches. Charging conspiracy without evidence of AGREEMENT (meetings, calls, money flow) is the classic over-charge.

refs.title: Possession of counterfeit currency / instruments
refs.plain: Counterfeit money and the tools to make it are separate offences.
refs.in_game: Counterfeit branch; document examination and fingerprint tests.

refs.title: Information in cognizable cases — the FIR
refs.plain: This is the birth of a case. If someone reports a serious (cognizable) crime, you MUST write it down, read it back to them, get their signature, and hand them a free copy. If you wrongly refuse, the complainant can go over your head to the SP.
refs.in_game: In the Duty Room you author the FIR narrative. The classifier checks it against the statutory ingredients of the offence. If you refuse to register a genuine cognizable offence, the complainant escalates to the SP and you lose Standing.

refs.title: Preliminary inquiry before registering an FIR
refs.plain: For middle-weight offences you may ask your SP for permission to spend up to 14 days checking whether there is really a case before you formally register it. It does NOT apply to the gravest offences.
refs.in_game: When the complaint is borderline, you may choose "Seek preliminary inquiry" instead of registering. It buys clarity but costs 14 days off your clock and can look like delay. Choosing wrongly is a scored decision.

refs.title: Inspection of the scene of occurrence
refs.plain: For serious offences you must physically inspect the scene yourself and record your inspection.
refs.in_game: Act 2 gating: the Crime Scene desk requires the arrival log, walk-through and scene diagram before exhibits can be lawfully collected.

refs.title: Inquest by police
refs.plain: For suspicious deaths, police hold a formal inquest and send the body for post-mortem.
refs.in_game: The Inquest step appears in Act 2 on the homicide branch. Completing it unlocks the post-mortem report as a lab item.

refs.title: When may police arrest without a warrant
refs.plain: Arrest without warrant is permitted for cognizable offences, but you must have reasonable suspicion — not a hunch.
refs.in_game: The arrest action in Act 5 is gated on the arrest-legality check. Arresting without recorded reasonable suspicion is a procedural violation that reduces your Standing and hands the defence an argument.

refs.title: Requirement of grounds for arrest
refs.plain: You cannot arrest casually. You must write down WHY the arrest was necessary.
refs.in_game: The Arrest Card requires you to type your grounds. The Legal Arbiter scores the entered grounds against the necessity test.

refs.title: Person arrested to be informed of grounds and right to bail
refs.plain: Inform the arrested person why he is being arrested and that he can seek bail.
refs.in_game: Arrest Card field. Leaving it blank creates a "procedural illegality" flag used against you in court.

refs.title: Search and seizure — independent witnesses
refs.plain: When you seize anything, two independent local witnesses must watch and sign the seizure list.
refs.in_game: THE most important handling rule in the game. A seizure memo with fewer than two witnesses sets exhibits.seizure_valid = 0, which taints the exhibit permanently. Witnesses typed into the memo are validated (not duplicated, not police).

refs.title: Charge sheet and the 60/90 day clock
refs.plain: You have 60 or 90 days to finish investigating and file your report. Miss it and the accused walks out on default bail.
refs.in_game: The HUD day-counter IS this section. Every action burns days. Interrogation, lab requests, surveillance all draw from the same clock. Exceeding day_limit closes the case as a default-bail failure.

refs.title: Report of Police Officer on completion of investigation
refs.plain: This is the charge sheet — the formal document that asks the court to try your accused. It must contain the parties, the case, your witnesses, the offence, and your annexures.
refs.in_game: The Charge Sheet Composer replicates this structure field-for-field. Missing annexures or a wrong accused list are blocking defects.

refs.title: Further investigation
refs.plain: Even after filing, you may keep investigating and file more evidence.
refs.in_game: Unlocked at higher ranks: you may reopen a closed case from the Case Wall if new evidence exists, for a time cost.

refs.title: Cognizance of offences by Magistrate
refs.plain: The court decides whether to accept your charge sheet and take up the case.
refs.in_game: Submitting your charge sheet triggers the cognizance check. A charge sheet with no admissible proof is rejected and returned for further investigation.

refs.title: Examination of accused
refs.plain: The court asks the accused to explain the evidence against him. This is the step where your proof must speak for itself.
refs.in_game: Act 8 stage. If your admissible evidence is thin, the accused simply denies everything and the doubt remains.

refs.title: Summons to produce documents or things
refs.plain: You can formally require a bank, telecom or shop to hand over records.
refs.in_game: Backs the CDR/financial/subpoena actions in Act 4: proper process raises the reliability of the pull.

refs.title: Confession to police officer not provable — the discovery rule
refs.plain: What the accused TELLS you is worthless in court. But if what he tells you leads you to recover a real object or fact, then just that part — the part that led to the discovery — becomes evidence.
refs.in_game: The single most important interrogation mechanic. Confessions are auto-filed as INADMISSIBLE. Only facts you convert into a witnessed RECOVERY survive. The Interrogation Room shows the split live.

refs.title: Chain of custody / continuous possession
refs.plain: You must be able to show the object passed hand to hand without a gap or a chance to tamper.
refs.in_game: Every exhibit carries a custody log. A missing hand-off, or an unlogged transfer, sets custody_intact = 0 and makes the exhibit contestable in court. The Lab Desk and Malkhana steps append to this log.

refs.title: Admissibility of electronic records — the certificate
refs.plain: Digital proof needs a special certificate (the s.63 certificate) signed by two people. Without it, the court will not even look at your CCTV, CDR or phone data.
refs.in_game: Digital exhibits must be hashed AND carry a dual-signed s.63 certificate before the Charge Sheet will accept them. The Cyber Cell operative or FSL digital-forensics expert signs. Missing certificate = inadmissible = cannot be listed.

refs.title: Electronic records as documents
refs.plain: Digital evidence is not weak evidence — but it must be certified.
refs.in_game: Supports the digital branch: a properly certified CCTV clip is high-weight evidence and carries real convictions.

refs.title: Opinion of expert — digital forensics
refs.plain: A qualified expert may give an opinion on technical matters.
refs.in_game: The FSL report carries an expert name and a skill-derived confidence. A low-skilled team produces low-confidence reports; a high-skill team can also SPOT overreach in a report.

refs.title: Opinion as to handwriting, finger impressions
refs.plain: Handwriting and fingerprint experts may opine on identity.
refs.in_game: Backs the Document Examination and Fingerprint lab tests; their reports feed the TIP and identity branch.

refs.title: Relevancy of facts forming part of the same transaction
refs.plain: Facts happening in the same event as the crime are relevant even if not the crime itself.
refs.in_game: Influence the Legal Arbiter: connected circumstances you have recorded raise the coherence of your narrative and the survivability of circumstantial cases.

refs.title: Facts necessary to explain or introduce relevant facts
refs.plain: Facts that give context — who is who, when and where — are relevant.
refs.in_game: Justifies the Identification Parade (TIP) step: identity evidence is admitted under this head.

refs.title: Presumption as to certain offences / abetment
refs.plain: Some facts can be presumed from surrounding circumstances.
refs.in_game: Narcotics and conspiracy branches lean on this; it rewards a properly assembled circumstantial file.
